title: Skateboarding Around the World and the Olympics
bigQuestion: What changed, and what stayed the same, when skateboarding spread around the world and joined the Olympic Games?

story.title: Thirteen on the Podium
story.kicker: In the summer of 2021, two thirteen-year-olds stood on an Olympic podium in Tokyo.
paragraphs: The skatepark at Ariake, on the Tokyo waterfront, is hot and nearly silent. The Games are being held in 2021, a year late, and spectators are not allowed in because of the pandemic. Cameras line the course. Coaches and teammates cheer from the edges, and the sound of urethane wheels on concrete fills the empty stands.

Momiji Nishiya of Japan is thirteen years old. She is in the first Olympic women's street final ever held. The course looks like a city plaza built by people who love skating: stairs, rails, ledges and banks. Some of the skaters she is competing against that summer are more than twice her age.

Her runs are steady. Then, in the single-trick rounds, she lands tricks down the long rail that score high with the judges. Across the course, Rayssa Leal of Brazil, also thirteen, is landing her own tricks with a grin. Funa Nakayama of Japan, sixteen, is close behind them both.

When the scores are final, Nishiya has gold, Leal silver and Nakayama bronze. Three teenagers stand on the podium. Back home, children in Japan and Brazil who watched on television carry their boards to the nearest curb.

Not every skater cheered the moment in the same way. Some felt that skating, a culture built in empty pools and city plazas, did not belong in a stadium with flags and anthems. Others felt that girls on a podium, watched around the world, opened a door that would not close.
story.think: Why might the same Olympic moment feel like a victory to some skaters and a loss to others?

lessons.title: Skateistan Begins in Kabul
lessons.mainIdea: Skateistan, founded by Oliver Percovich in Kabul in 2007, used skateboarding to draw children, including many girls, into education.
reading: Oliver Percovich, a skater from Australia, arrived in Kabul, Afghanistan, in 2007 with a few skateboards. When he rode in the streets, children crowded around and asked to try. Many of them worked on the streets selling goods and did not go to school. Percovich noticed that girls were joining in as well.

In 2007 he founded *Skateistan*, a nonprofit organization. A *nonprofit* is a group that uses any money it raises for its mission rather than paying owners. Skateistan's idea was simple. Skateboarding would be the hook. Children who came to skate would also join classes in reading, art and other subjects, and some would be helped back into regular school.

Skateistan built an indoor skatepark in Kabul so that girls could skate in a space where families felt comfortable sending them. Girls made up a large share of its students. At the time, few sports were open to girls in Afghanistan, and skateboarding was so new that no one had yet decided it was only for boys.

words.d: a nonprofit founded in Kabul, Afghanistan, in 2007 by Oliver Percovich that uses skateboarding to bring children into education
an organization that uses the money it raises for its mission instead of paying it to owners
the main purpose an organization works toward

lessons.title: Growing Beyond Kabul
lessons.mainIdea: Skateistan spread to other countries, won wide attention, and had to change its work in Afghanistan after 2021.
reading: Skateistan grew beyond Kabul. It opened programs in other Afghan cities and later in Cambodia and South Africa, following the same pattern of skating plus education. Each program hired local staff, and many former students became coaches and teachers themselves. This model, where people who learned in a program go on to lead it, helps a project last.

In 2020 a short documentary about Skateistan's girls, Learning to Skateboard in a Warzone (If You're a Girl), won the Academy Award for best documentary short. The film followed young students in Kabul as they learned to skate and to drop in on a ramp, and as they went to class. Its win brought the program to millions of new viewers.

In August 2021 the Taliban returned to power in Afghanistan and placed strict limits on girls' education. Skateistan had to change how it worked there, and many of its public programs could not continue as before. The story shows both the power of a simple idea and how much it depends on the world around it.

Skateistan is one of many programs worldwide that use skating for *youth development*, which means helping young people build skills, confidence and connections. Similar groups work in cities on several continents, often in places with few parks or youth programs.

lessons.title: Joining the Olympic Program
lessons.mainIdea: The International Olympic Committee added skateboarding in 2016 for the Tokyo Games, which were held in 2021.
reading: The *International Olympic Committee*, or IOC, decides which sports appear at the Olympic Games. In 2016 it approved five new sports for the Tokyo 2020 Games: skateboarding, surfing, sport climbing, karate, and baseball and softball. The Tokyo organizers had proposed them, partly to draw younger viewers.

Each Olympic sport needs an *international federation*, a body that writes the rules and organizes qualifying events around the world. For skateboarding that body is World Skate, which also governs roller sports. Skaters earned their places through a ranking system based on contests held before the Games.

The COVID-19 pandemic pushed the Tokyo Games back by one year. They were held in the summer of 2021 but kept the name Tokyo 2020. Skateboarding took place at Ariake Urban Sports Park on the Tokyo waterfront. Because of the pandemic, spectators were not allowed, so most people watched on television and online.

lessons.title: Street and Park
lessons.mainIdea: Olympic skateboarding has two kinds of events: street, on a course like a city plaza, and park, in a deep, curved bowl.
reading: Olympic skateboarding has four events: men's and women's street, and men's and women's park. In *street*, skaters ride a course built to look like a city plaza, with stairs, handrails, ledges, banks and curbs. The tricks are mostly ollies, flips, grinds and slides on these obstacles.

In *park*, skaters ride a bowl, a deep concrete basin with curved walls called transitions. The style grows from the empty swimming pools that skaters rode in California in the 1970s. Park riders pump to build speed, fly above the top edge, called the coping, and spin or grab the board in the air.

Each event has its own format. In general, street skaters take timed runs across the course and also try single tricks, one at a time, and only their best scores count. Park skaters take a few timed runs, and their best run counts. Formats have been adjusted between Games, but the idea of runs plus best scores has stayed.

These are skilled athletes at the top of the sport, riding at a skatepark built for the event. The stairs and handrails on a street course are for experts with years of training. New skaters build up on flat ground, small curbs and low ramps first, with a helmet and pads.

lessons.title: How Judges Score
lessons.mainIdea: Judges score difficulty, clean landings, height and speed, and variety, and height in the air follows simple physics.
reading: Skateboarding has no finish line or goal, so a panel of judges gives scores. They look at how hard each trick is, how cleanly it is done and landed, how high and fast the skater rides, how varied the tricks are, and how well a run flows from one trick to the next. A fall or a sketchy landing, where the skater wobbles or touches down, lowers the score.

Height is one thing the judges can see clearly, and it follows the physics of falling. Once a skater leaves the coping, gravity is the main force acting. The skater rises, slows, stops for an instant at the top and falls back. The *air time*, the total time off the ramp, for a jump that rises h meters above the coping is about 2√(2h/g).

Here is a worked example with g = 9.8 m/s². For an air 1.0 m above the coping: 2h/g = 2 × 1.0 ÷ 9.8, which is about 0.204. The square root of 0.204 is about 0.452. Doubling gives about 0.90 seconds. For 2.0 m: 2 × 2.0 ÷ 9.8 is about 0.408, its square root is about 0.639, and doubling gives about 1.28 seconds.

Notice that doubling the height does not double the air time. Air time grows with the square root of height. That extra time is what lets a park skater fit in a full spin or a long grab, which is why height and difficulty often go together on the judges' sheets.

words.d: the time a skater spends off the ramp or ground during a jump

how cleanly and smoothly a trick is done and landed

lessons.title: Street Gold in Tokyo
lessons.mainIdea: At Tokyo 2020, Yuto Horigome and Momiji Nishiya of Japan won the first Olympic street gold medals, and Rayssa Leal of Brazil took silver at thirteen.
reading: The men's street final was the first Olympic skateboarding event ever held, in July 2021. Yuto Horigome of Japan won the gold medal. Horigome grew up in Tokyo, so he won the first skateboarding gold in his home city. He was known for technical tricks on rails and ledges, where the board must lock in precisely.

The women's street final came the next day. Momiji Nishiya of Japan, thirteen years old, won gold. Rayssa Leal of Brazil, also thirteen, won silver. Funa Nakayama of Japan, sixteen, took bronze. It was one of the youngest podiums in Olympic history. Leal had become famous years earlier when a video of her as a small child, skating in a fairy costume, spread widely online, and Brazilians call her Fadinha, "little fairy."

The street results showed how far skating had spread. Japan and Brazil both have large, active skate scenes. A *medalist* is any athlete who wins a gold, silver or bronze medal. Street medalists in Tokyo came from Japan, Brazil and the United States, a mix that would have been hard to imagine when skating's first contests were held in California in the 1960s.

the raised stand where the top three finishers receive their medals

lessons.title: Park Gold in Tokyo
lessons.mainIdea: In the Tokyo park events, Sakura Yosozumi of Japan and Keegan Palmer of Australia won gold, and Sky Brown won bronze for Great Britain at thirteen.
reading: The women's park final put three teenagers on the podium again. Sakura Yosozumi of Japan, nineteen, won gold. Kokona Hiraki of Japan, twelve, won silver. Sky Brown of Great Britain, thirteen, won bronze. Brown was born in Japan to a Japanese mother and a British father and chose to compete for Great Britain.

Brown's medal came after a serious training fall in 2020, when she came off a ramp and was badly hurt. She recovered in time to compete at the Games the next summer. Her story drew attention to how much risk park skaters face in the air, and to the role of helmets and careful progression even for experts.

In the men's park final, Keegan Palmer of Australia won gold with high, fast runs through the bowl. Park rewards *amplitude*, the height a skater reaches above the coping, along with spins, grabs and flips done at that height. Pedro Barros of Brazil took silver, adding to Brazil's medals in the sport.

lessons.title: Paris 2024 and Beyond
lessons.mainIdea: At Paris 2024, Horigome and Palmer won gold again, Arisa Trew and Coco Yoshizawa won the women's titles, and skating is set for Los Angeles 2028.
reading: For the Paris 2024 Games, skateboarding moved to the center of the city. The course was built at the Place de la Concorde, a famous square, alongside BMX freestyle and breaking. The setting matched skating's roots in public plazas, though this plaza was fenced, ticketed and built for the event.

Two Tokyo champions won again. Yuto Horigome of Japan took men's street gold, and Keegan Palmer of Australia took men's park gold. Defending a title is hard in any sport, and in skating the tricks needed to win grow harder every year. A *defending champion* is the winner of the last contest who competes to win again.

New names won the women's events. Coco Yoshizawa of Japan won women's street gold, and Rayssa Leal of Brazil added a bronze to her Tokyo silver. Arisa Trew of Australia won women's park gold. Sky Brown of Great Britain won bronze in park again. Skateboarding is on the program for the Los Angeles 2028 Games, returning the Olympic sport to California, where so much of its history began.

words.d: the winner of the last contest, competing to win the title again

lessons.title: Contests Before the Olympics
lessons.mainIdea: Skateboarding contests began long before the Olympics, from Anaheim in 1965 to Del Mar in 1975 to the X Games.
reading: Skaters argue about the Olympics as if contests were new, but they are nearly as old as the sport. The first National Skateboard Championships were held in Anaheim, California, in 1965 and shown on ABC's Wide World of Sports. Patti McGee won the women's title and appeared on the cover of Life magazine that year.

In 1975 the Del Mar Nationals in California became famous for the Zephyr team from Santa Monica and Venice. Skaters such as Peggy Oki, Tony Alva, Jay Adams and Stacy Peralta rode low and fast, copying surf moves on the slalom and freestyle courses. Their style shocked judges used to upright, stiff riding, and it changed how skating looked.

In 1995 the cable channel ESPN held the Extreme Games in Rhode Island, renamed the X Games from 1996. Tony Hawk landed the 900, two and a half spins in the air, at the 1999 X Games in San Francisco. These events built a *competitive* side of skating, with prize money, sponsors and television, long before the IOC took notice.

lessons.title: The Olympic Debate
lessons.mainIdea: Skaters disagree about the Olympics: some see lost freedom and culture, others see money, parks and new doors for girls and young skaters.
reading: When the IOC added skateboarding, many skaters were unhappy. They saw skating as closer to art or music than to a sport. To them, its heart was style, creativity and freedom: riding a spot no one else noticed, filming a part with friends, inventing a trick. They worried that national teams, coaches, uniforms and judges with scoring sheets would turn that into a checklist.

Another concern was control. Skaters had built their own companies, magazines and videos for decades. Some resented that an outside federation, which also runs roller sports, would set the rules. There were also worries about pressure on very young athletes chasing medals.

Supporters answered with results. Olympic status brought government money for skateparks and coaching in many countries. It showed girls skating on a world stage, and the Tokyo podiums inspired new riders in Japan, Brazil and beyond. Many top skaters chose to compete and said the Games let them represent their families and hometowns.

Most skaters today hold a middle view. The Olympics are one part of skateboarding, not the whole thing. Videos, street spots, local parks and DIY builds go on as before. A *subculture*, a group with its own values and style inside a larger society, can join the mainstream and still keep its own life.

lessons.title: Young Champions, Long Careers
lessons.mainIdea: Young Olympic skaters train with protection and step-by-step progression, and their careers depend on recovering well from falls.
reading: Many Olympic skaters started riding before age ten. Medical groups such as the American Academy of Pediatrics advise that children under five should not ride skateboards and that children six to ten should be supervised by an adult. Young skaters who reach a high level usually grow up with coaches, parents and older skaters watching closely.

Top skaters fall often. Practicing a hard trick can mean dozens of attempts. Learning to fall small helps: crouching low, rolling with the fall, sliding on knee pads on a ramp, and not catching the body with locked straight arms. Wrist injuries are among the most common skateboarding injuries, and wrist guards help prevent them.

Park skaters fly above the coping, so a fall can come from well over a meter higher than the ramp's edge. A *helmet* that fits snugly and is buckled is standard equipment in the bowl. Sky Brown's 2020 training fall and her return to win medals showed both the danger of the event and how much careful recovery matters.

For anyone inspired by the Games, the path is the same one the champions took. Start with a helmet, pads and flat shoes on smooth ground. Learn to push, stop and turn. Move to small ramps and low curbs at a skatepark. The tricks seen at the Olympics come after years of steady practice.
